excerpt: Percent just means 'out of 100' — and once that clicks, the whole Class 6 percentage chapter falls into place. Here is the chapter walked through with rupee examples, two solved shop case studies, and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A shopkeeper writes ‘20% off’ on a board, and half the customers still cannot say what they will actually pay. That gap — between reading a percent and using one — is exactly what the class 6 maths percentage chapter is built to close. The idea underneath it is small enough to fit in one line: percent means out of 100. Everything else in the chapter, from converting fractions to working out a discount at the market, is just that one idea wearing different clothes.

I have taught this chapter to a fair number of Tier-2 city sixth-graders, and the ones who sail through are never the fastest calculators. They are the ones who genuinely believe that 25% and one-quarter are the same thing. Get the child to that belief and the sums stop being scary.

What ‘per cent’ actually means

The word comes from the Latin per centum — for every hundred. So 37% is simply 37 out of 100, or the fraction 37/100. That is the whole definition. When a child writes 37% = 37/100, they have already done the hardest part.

A neat way to make it real: draw a 10×10 grid of 100 squares. Shade 37 of them. That shaded patch is 37%. Ask ‘how many are not shaded?’ and the child discovers 63% without being told the rule that percentages of a whole add to 100.

Converting between fractions, decimals and percents

This is the engine room of the chapter. Three forms, one value, and you must be able to move between any two of them.

  • Percent to fraction: put it over 100 and simplify. 40% = 40/100 = 2/5.
  • Fraction to percent: multiply by 100. 3/4 = (3/4) × 100 = 75%.
  • Percent to decimal: divide by 100 (move the point two places left). 65% = 0.65.
  • Decimal to percent: multiply by 100. 0.08 = 8%.

Here is the conversion table I ask every student to memorise cold. These few come up again and again, and knowing them by heart saves real time in an exam.

The one conversion students get wrong

Watch the direction of the decimal shift. Going from a percent to a decimal you move the point left (65% becomes 0.65); going the other way you move it right. More than half the silly mistakes in this chapter are a decimal point that travelled the wrong way.

Finding a percent of a quantity

This is the skill that pays off outside the classroom. To find a percentage of a number, turn the percent into a fraction or decimal and multiply. What is 15% of ₹600? Either 15/100 × 600 = 90, or 0.15 × 600 = 90. So 15% of ₹600 is ₹90.

The mental shortcut worth teaching: 10% of anything is just that number with the decimal shifted one place — 10% of ₹850 is ₹85. From there, 5% is half of the 10%, and 20% is double it. A child who owns the 10% trick can estimate most discounts in their head at the shop.

Commercial maths: profit, loss and discount

Now the chapter turns to money, which is where percentages earn their keep. A few terms first, all in rupees:

  • Cost price (CP) — what the seller paid.
  • Selling price (SP) — what the buyer paid.
  • Profit = SP − CP, when SP is more.
  • Loss = CP − SP, when SP is less.

The percentage is always worked out on the cost price in this chapter. Profit% = (Profit / CP) × 100. That ‘divide by CP’ is the detail examiners love to test, so drill it.

Discount is the twin idea, but it hangs off the marked price (MP) — the printed price before any reduction. Discount = MP − SP, and Discount% = (Discount / MP) × 100. There is even a gentle first look at simple interest: earn a fixed percent on money kept in a bank each year. Class 6 usually keeps this to the idea rather than the full formula, so do not overload a child here.

Case study 1: the stationery bill

Riya buys a geometry box marked ₹250 with a 20% discount. How much does she pay?

Discount = 20% of 250 = 0.20 × 250 = ₹50. So she pays 250 − 50 = ₹200. A quicker route: paying after a 20% cut means paying 80%, and 80% of 250 = 0.80 × 250 = ₹200. Same answer, one step fewer.

Case study 2: the fruit-seller’s profit

A vendor buys a crate of mangoes for ₹400 and sells the lot for ₹500. What is the profit percent?

Profit = 500 − 400 = ₹100. Profit% = (100 / 400) × 100 = 25%. Notice the division is by 400, the cost price — not by 500. Divide by the wrong number and you get 20%, the classic trap. These are the kinds of real-bill passages the case-study workbook builds on, with the working shown line by line.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

The eight questions below cover exactly what we walked through — converting forms, finding a percent of an amount, and simple profit, loss and discount. Attempt them, then read the explanations for any you miss. questions.q: What does 45% mean as a fraction before simplifying?
questions.explanation: Percent means out of 100, so 45% is 45/100.

faq.q: What does percentage mean in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: Percentage means ‘out of 100’. So 30% is 30 out of every 100, which is the fraction 30/100. Every question in the chapter builds on that single idea.

faq.q: How do I convert a fraction to a percentage?
faq.a: Multiply the fraction by 100. For example, 2/5 × 100 = 40%, so 2/5 is the same as 40%. To go back, put the percent over 100 and simplify.

faq.q: How do I find a percent of a number, like 15% of ₹600?
faq.a: Turn the percent into a decimal or fraction and multiply. 15% of ₹600 is 0.15 × 600 = ₹90. A handy trick is that 10% is just the number with the decimal shifted one place left.

faq.q: How is profit percent calculated in Class 6?
faq.a: First find the profit, which is selling price minus cost price. Then Profit% = (Profit / Cost Price) × 100. The common mistake is dividing by the selling price instead of the cost price.
